lead: Alfred Russel Wallace: 1864 'Origin of Human Races' vs the 1869/1870 'Limits of Natural Selection as applied to Man'
reason: Both pieces are chapters IX and X of the same book (Contributions, Gutenberg #22428), and chapter X opens by announcing limits to natural selection without saying he now disagrees with his 1864 paper; grepping Darwinism (#14558), Island Life (#32021) and the Geographical Distribution of Animals for a retraction found only a 1889 remark that he 'then believed' he could demonstrate natural selection accumulating infertility (no earlier text of his stating it).

lead: Coleridge: Biographia Literaria (1817, Gutenberg #6081) vs early politics and Unitarian religion (Conciones ad Populum 1795, The Watchman 1796)
reason: The announcement is real and explicit (Biographia: 'I was at that time and long after ... a zealous Unitarian ... My opinions were indeed in many and most important points erroneous'), but the only English scans of his early prose found (archive.org concionesadpopul00cole, 1795, and cu31924103990358, The Watchman 1796) are prints whose OCR reads the long s as f ('fhould', 'fuch', 'Defpotifm'), so no clean verbatim early passage could be taken; the 1850 Essays on His Own Times (which reprints the Watchman essays in modern type) was not tried.

lead: Whewell: Astronomy and General Physics (Bridgewater Treatise III, 1833, Gutenberg #66406) vs Of the Plurality of Worlds (1853, Gutenberg #36288)
reason: The 1833 text only conjectures that the planets may be inhabited ('To conjecture is all that we can do'), and the anonymous 1853 preface and essay never say he changed his mind about it.

lead: Oscar Wilde: Intentions (1891, Gutenberg #887) vs De Profundis (Gutenberg #921) on pleasure and sorrow
reason: De Profundis announces it clearly ('I used to live entirely for pleasure. I shunned suffering and sorrow of every kind ... I could not understand it'), but the early essays are dialogues, so no passage is Wilde's own statement of the early thesis (the lines belong to Vivian, Gilbert or Cyril).

lead: Max Mueller: 'Aryan race' in the Lectures on the Science of Language (Gutenberg #32856) vs Biographies of Words and the Home of the Aryas (1888)
reason: The 1888 text (archive.org OCR only) says 'There is no Aryan race in blood ... Aryan ... means language and nothing but language' but presents this as what he has always said ('I have declared again and again'), so there is no passage where he admits an earlier different view.

lead: G. H. Lewes: Biographical History of Philosophy (Comtist, 1857) vs Problems of Life and Mind (1874-79)
reason: Only Google-scan OCR on archive.org (problemslifeand00unkngoog, biographicalhis05lewegoog), noisy with 'Digitized by Google' and broken words; a grep of the 1874 volume found no statement that he abandoned his earlier view of metaphysics.

lead: Joseph Priestley: Memoirs (written 1795, Gutenberg #75111) vs an earlier Arian-period work
reason: The announcement is explicit and states the new view ('By reading with care Dr. Lardner's letter on the logos, I became what is called a Socinian soon after my settlement at Leeds'), but a clean early text stating the Arian view was not found: the pre-1768 tracts exist only inside Rutt's 1817 Works (archive.org OCR volumes of 1.5 MB each) and I could not locate the volume or passage in the time available.

lead: William Lloyd Garrison: 1829 Park Street address (pro-colonization) vs Thoughts on African Colonization (1832, Gutenberg #31178)
reason: The 1832 book announces the change in his own words ('I formerly supposed the Colonization Society was a praiseworthy association ... whereas I was then blind, now I see'), but the 1829 address is not available as a standalone text (it is not in the 1852 Selections; it survives only quoted in the 1885 biography by his children), and he says it contained 'only a single sentence in favor of the Society'.

lead: Ruskin: any thesis in Fors Clavigera (Gutenberg vols 1-4, 6) vs Modern Painters or Stones of Venice
reason: Searched five Fors volumes for self-corrections ('I was wrong', 'mistaken', 'I retract' near titles of his earlier books) and found none that retract a stated thesis.

lead: Charles Darwin: Voyage of the Beagle (Gutenberg #944) vs the Autobiography on feelings of the sublime and belief in more in man than the body (and the religion passage)
reason: The Gutenberg Autobiography (#2010, the abridged 1887 text) does not include the religion section that quotes his Journal and says he no longer has those convictions, so the announcement is missing; the Glen Roy case was used instead.

lead: Henry C. Carey: free trade (Essay on the Rate of Wages, 1835) vs protectionism (Harmony of Interests, 1851)
reason: Biographies describe a shift, but a web search found no passage in which Carey himself repudiates the earlier view; not pursued further.

lead: Comte (Positive Philosophy vs Positive Polity), Gibbon (Memoirs), Harriet Martineau (Autobiography), Tolstoy, Leslie Stephen, Burke, Paine, Southey, Mivart, Haeckel
reason: Only availability was checked, and only partly: Gutenberg has Comte's General View of Positivism and the French Cours but not the Positive Philosophy or Positive Polity in English; Gibbon's Memoirs (#6031) is a retrospective and I did not find a clean English text of his early work; a Gutenberg search found no Martineau Autobiography, no early Southey prose and no later Mivart work (Southey and Mivart as in the earlier agent's note, not rechecked); Tolstoy's What Is Art? (#64908) was located but no early passage was looked for; no documented announced retraction was identified for Stephen, Burke or Paine.

lead: Not pursued: Royce, Mach, Jevons, Marshall, Henry George, Kingsley, Carlyle, Matthew Arnold, Asa Gray, Thomas Arnold, Paley, Augustine (Retractations)
reason: No documented retraction of a specific thesis was identified within the search budget; stopped after six verified cases (two of them on one author's two works with different theses).
